newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand reassures market on baht, other centres nervous.
newsitem.headline: Thailand reassures market on baht, other centres nervous.

text.p: Thailand on Thursday reassured investors about the embattled baht, dismissing market talk that it may be devalued, as some of its nervous Asian neighbours moved to protect their own currencies from speculative attacks.
"The central bank would like to ask the private sector to have confidence in the government policy and not to listen to the rumours," the Bank of Thailand said in a statement received on Thursday.
"The central bank wishes to stress that there would be no devaluation or changes in the currency exchange mechanism which were mentioned by rumours," it said.

Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan on Thursday also reiterated the government's determination to guard the currency against speculative attacks. He said the government's defense of the baht has been, and will be successful.

Rising concerns about the slowing Thai economy and rumours of political turmoil in the cabinet that could lead to Amnuay's possible resignation triggered heavy baht sales for the dollar on Wednesday. Amnuay has repeatedly denied he would quit.
"(On Wednesday) there was fierce speculation on the baht in the overseas market," the central bank statement said. "At present the situation has eased to a certain degree."

The central bank and the Monetary Authority of Singapore jointly intervened in the foreign exchange market on Wednesday to defend the baht. Malaysia's central bank and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority also bought the Thai currency.

Amnuay said on Thursday that Thailand has support "from all our friends" in its currency defense. He also moved to soothe fears about the deterioration in the Thai economy, saying the country was "in a process of recovery."
The economy had gone through its worst, Amnuary said, noting he was pleased with a sharp decline in the current account deficit and inflation, as well as expectations that exports were improving.
The market rumours also hit the Thai bourse on Wednesday, causing the market to drop to near eight-year lows. The main index closed at 571.30 points, a fall of 4.82 percent.
Brokers expected trading to remain cautious on Thursday with continued foreign selling likely on persistent concerns about the battered baht.
The Thai baht was firmer in early dealings on Thursday. The currency was at 25.910/940 at 0245 GMT, compared with around 26.330/26.430 in late dealings on Wednesday.
Thailand's currency woes have unnerved other markets in the region with the Philippine peso and Malaysian ringgit suffering heavy selling on Wednesday.

The Philippines Central Bank said it had raised overnight interest rates by 0.75 percentage points to 12 percent in what it said was a preemptive move in case there is any spillover from the problems in Thailand.
The bank said it was prepared to boost interest rates again to protect the peso.
The country's stock market, particularly the property sector, had also been dented recently by concerns that Thailand's troubles could be duplicated in the Philippines.
"We will continue to raise interest rates if there will be speculation on the peso," Central Bank Treasurer Sergio Edeza told Reuters.
The bank also sold about $70 million in early trades at 26.375 pesos on Thursday following the rate hike, traders said.
The peso was at 26.368/26.370 at 0245 GMT with traded volume heavy at $94 million.
The Malaysian ringgit recovered slightly in early Thursday trading as players tooks profits on dollar/ringgit positions.
But traders warned that dollar demand would weigh on the local currency and fears of further intervention by Bank Negara Malaysia was limiting activity.
The central bank intervened strongly at 2.5250 ringgit on Wednesday to cap the dollar's rise. At 0245 GMT, the ringgit was at 2.5177/87 to the dollar against Wednesday's close of 2.5240/50.
The Indonesian rupiah was also soft, mainly on fears of violence in the current general election campaign but also due to a spill-over from attacks on the baht.
